Design and development of letrozole nanoemulsion: A comparative
evaluation of brain targeted nanoemulsion with free letrozole against status
epilepticus and neurodegeneration in mice

Nanoemulsion

A B S T R A C T
The target of the current study is to formulate letrozole loaded nanoemulsion (LET-NE) for the direct nose to
brain delivery to reduce peripheral effects of letrozole (LET). LET-NE is compared against intraperitoneally
administered free LET in kainic acid (KA) induced status epilepticus (SE) in mice. LET loaded nanoemulsion
(LET-NE) was prepared by aqueous microtitration method using Triacetin, Tween 80 and PEG-400 as the oil
phase, surfactant, and co-surfactant. Nanoemulsion was studied for droplet size, polydispersity index (PDI), zeta
potential, percentage transmittance, drug content, surface morphology. TEM images of developed formulation
demonstrated spherical droplets with a mean diameter of 95.59 ± 2.34 nm, PDI of 0.162 ± 0.012 and zeta
potential of −7.12 ± 0.12 mV respectively. In in-vitro and ex-vivo drug release, LET-NE showed prolonged drug
release profile as compared to suspension. SE was induced by KA (10 mg/kg, i.p.) in Swiss albino mice.
Behavioral seizure monitoring, biochemical estimations, and histopathological examination were performed.
The onset time of SE was significantly enhanced and % incidence of SE was reduced by intranasal administration
of LET-NE as compared to KA and LET administered intraperitoneally. Biochemical estimations revealed that
LET-NE effectively decreased levels of 17-β estradiol while the levels of 5α-Dihydrotestosterone (5α-DHT) and
3α-androstanediol (3α-Diol) were significantly increased in the hippocampus. In cresyl violet staining LET-NE
showed better protection of the hippocampus from neurotoxicity induced by KA as compared to LET. Also, in
gamma scintigraphy of mouse brain, intranasal administration of nanoemulsion exhibited the presence of high
concentration of LET. The study demonstrates the anticonvulsant and neuroprotective effect of LET-NE probably
by inhibition of aromatization of testosterone into 17-β estradiol, proconvulsant, and diverting the pathway into
the synthesis of testosterone metabolites, 3α-Diol with known anticonvulsant and neuroprotective action. Brain
targeting of LET-NE showed better anticonvulsant and neuroprotective action than LET.
1. Introduction
Status epilepticus (SE) is a serious neurological condition char-
acterized by persistent episodes of seizures (Fisher et al., 2014). World
Health Organization (WHO) forecast that worldwide 50 million people
at present live with epilepsy, and roughly 2.4 million people are iden-
tified to suffer from epilepsy annually (WHO, 2018). However, despite
the development of new antiepileptic drug therapy, more than one-
third of patients of SE suffer from refractory epilepsy (WHO, 2018).
Therefore, there is a serious need to identify newer targets for the
treatment of SE.
Neurosteroids are a group of steroid hormones produced de novo in
the brain from precursor cholesterol into distinct neurosteroids (Reddy,
2004a). Neurosteroids play a leading act in the neuroendocrine role of
brain excitability, seizure susceptibility, and pathogenesis of epilepsy
by transforming into distinct metabolites such as allopregnanolone,
allotetrahydrodeoxycorticosterone, estradiol, and androstenediol. Tes-
tosterone is metabolized by the 5α-reductase enzyme to intermediate

5α-dihydrotestosterone (5α-DHT), which later reduces to form 3α-an-
drostanediol (3α-Diol) using 3α-hydroxysteroid oxidoreductase (3α-
HSOR). Aromatase is the major enzyme which converts testosterone
into 17β-estradiol in the brain as well as in peripheral tissues (Martini
et al., 1993). 17β-estradiol has seizure enhancing properties and leads
to neuronal excitability. Aromatase is present in distinct regions of the
brain such as hippocampus and neocortex, areas linked with SE. First
generation aromatase inhibitors, aminoglutethimide, and testolactone
have been used as an antiepileptic drug in conjunction with another
antiepileptic drugs in patients with resistant seizures, which suggests
that aromatase inhibitors might be useful in the management of sei-
zures (Aguilar et al., 1961). It has been reported that few clinically used
antiepileptic drugs, for example, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, tiagabine,
phenobarbital, phenytoin, ethosuximide, and valproate inhibits ar-
omatase enzyme and that the inhibitory effects varied from 1.4 to
49.7 mM. Further, antiepileptic drugs such as phenytoin, phenobarbital,
valproic acid, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, etc. were also found to have
over 70% structural and chemical similarities with aromatase in-
hibitors, strengthening the fact that aromatase inhibitors may have
antiepileptic potential (Jacobsen et al., 2008; Muftuoglu and Mustata,
2011). LET and anastrozole, are the third generation non-steroidal ar-
omatase inhibitors approved by US-FDA, for the treatment of breast
cancer in the postmenopausal woman (NIH, 2013). In a pilot study,
anastrozole has also been tested as an add-on treatment for men suf-
fering from intractable epilepsy (Harden and MacLusky, 2005). Re-
cently, we demonstrated the anticonvulsant effect of LET against kainic
acid (KA) induced seizures in mice (Iqbal et al., 2018). Few preclinical
studies also showed the protective effect of an aromatase inhibitor, LET
in the prevention of seizures induced by pentylenetetrazole and kainic
acid in mice (Rashid et al., 2015; Reddy, 2004b). In a clinical report,
LET has been revealed to attenuate seizures in a 61-year-old male pa-
tient suffering from temporal lobe epilepsy in addition to standard
antiepileptic drugs (Harden and MacLusky, 2004, 2005). Hence, in
forthcoming, aromatase inhibition may be a valuable remedy for males
enduring both testosterone insufficiency and SE. However, there are
various peripheral adverse effects of LET that might limit its potential
use in epilepsy. The side effects of aromatase inhibitors that affect the
central nervous system (CNS) includes hot flushes, headache, dizziness,
depression, anxiety, insomnia whereas peripheral side effects of ar-
omatase inhibitors are hyperglycemia, pain in muscles, hair loss, rash,
vaginal bleeding, dry skin, and hypertension. One of the major per-
ipheral adverse effects, as reported by various clinical and preclinical
studies, is that aromatase inhibitors cause increased bone loss enhan-
cing the risk of bone fractures in women with breast cancer (Erbağ
et al., 2015; Yonden et al., 2009). Development of brain-targeted for-
mulation of aromatase inhibitor can precede to targeted drug delivery
in the brain, enhanced the therapeutic action, dose reduction and can
minimize the peripheral side effects.
Delivery of therapeutic agents directly to the brain is restricted by
barriers like a blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-cerebrospinal fluid
barrier (Blasi et al., 2007). The intranasal route is the promising ap-
proach to deliver therapeutic agents directly to the brain for active
molecules that cannot enter the brain by other routes by eluding BBB
and decreasing drug delivery to non-targeted sites (Gulam et al., 2012).
Intranasal route delivers drug via olfactory and trigeminal nerve
pathways through the nasal cribriform plate (Talegaonkar and Mishra,
2004). Intranasal drug delivery has several advantages, such as the
prevention of gastrointestinal degradation, hepatic first-pass metabo-
lism, reduced toxicity, ease of administration as compared to other
routes such as intravenous, intramuscular routes and higher bioavail-
ability at a lower dose (Illum, 2003). Various current epileptic drugs
such as diazepam, clonazepam, midazolam are in clinical trials for the
treatment of emergency seizure using the intranasal route for drug
delivery (Kapoor et al., 2016).
Nanoemulsion (NE) is isotropic, thermodynamically stable systems
of water, oil, surfactants, and co-surfactants, which go through
spontaneous emulsification in aqueous fluids to form an oil in water
emulsion. NE offers several advantages, including high kinetic stability,
high solvent capacity, increased solubility and permeability of drugs
(Gong et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013). Further, they have been shown
as a suitable delivery system for the nose to brain drug targeting owing
to their lipophilic nature and small globule size (Acharya et al., 2013).
Intranasal administration of NE is a favorable method for brain-targeted
drug delivery.
The present work, therefore, aimed to utilize nanotechnology to
formulate NE of LET for the nose to brain delivery and was evaluated
for various in vitro parameters. Further, LET-NE was assessed for an-
ticonvulsant and neuroprotective effects and was compared against free
LET in KA-induced SE in mice. Intranasal drug delivery might result in
enhanced drug bioavailability in the brain with the reduced peripheral
side effects. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to report
the NE as a drug delivery system for LET, with it’s in vitro and in vivo
evaluation.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
LET was received as a gift sample from Ind-Swift Laboratories,
India. Tween 80 and dialysis membrane-70 (LA 393-1 MT) were pur-
chased from Himedia (India). Polyethylene glycol 400 (PEG-400), HPLC
grade methanol, and HPLC grade water were procured from Thomas
Baker, Merck and Loba Chemie (India) respectively. KA was purchased
from Cayman Chemicals, U.S.A. Other chemicals and solvents used
were of analytical grade. 17β-estradiol, 5α-Dihydrotestosterone (5α-
DHT) and 3α-androstanediol (3α-Diol) mouse specific Elisa kits were
purchased from Sincere Biotech (China).
2.2. Experimental methods
2.2.1. Screening of excipients
For formulation development, selection of oil, surfactant, and co-
surfactant was characteristically important. The crucial selection of oil
and surfactants was done based on the solubility of LET in them.
Miscibility of selected oil with the surfactants was the other parameter
based on which surfactant and co-surfactant were confirmed.
For solubility of LET, oils selected were oleic acid, eucalyptus oil,
labrafac, triacetin, black seed oil, isopropyl myristate, capyrol 90,
captex 200P, captex 500P. The surfactants opt for solubility study were
Tween 80, Tween 20, PEG-400, span 80, span 20, plurol oleique CC 497
CG and transcutol P. The selection of the oils and surfactant was done
on the basis of their easy obtainability and biodegradability.
The solubility of LET was determined by adding a large quantity of
LET in a microcentrifuge tube (MCT) comprising 1 ml solvent (oil or
surfactant) and the mixture was shaken for in room temperature
(25 ± 1 °C) at 72 h with the help of Remi CM-101 cyclomixer. Later,
the mixture was centrifuged (Remi R8C Laboratory Centrifuge) at
3000 rpm for 10–15 min. The supernatant was taken in another tube
and diluted up to 1 ml with methanol (Hosny and Banjar, 2013). The
absorbance was taken at 240 nm afterward appropriate dilution and,
the unknown amount of LET dissolved in that specific oil or surfactant
was calculated by previously created calibration plot (Parveen et al.,
2011).
2.2.2. Preparation of phase diagrams
The pseudoternary phase diagrams of oil, surfactant, co-surfactant,
and water were developed using the aqueous titration method to obtain
the NE region. Furthermore, to optimize the ratio of surfactant and co-
surfactant, different ratios of Smix (1:1, 2:1, 3:1 and 4:1) were taken. For
each, phase diagram, the ratio of oil to the Smix were varied as 1:9, 1:8,
1:7, 1:6, 1:5, 1:3.5, 1:3, 1:2, 2:8, 3:7, 4:6, 5:5, 6:4, 7:3, 8:2 and 9:1.
Water was added drop-wise to each Oil–Smix mixture under vigorous

2.2.3. Formula optimization of placebo nanoemulsion
The clear/transparent placebo formulations obtained from phase
diagrams were taken for further study. Thermodynamic stability studies
such as the heating-cooling cycle and freeze-thaw test were done to
reject metastable NE formulation. In addition, physical stability study
(centrifugation test) was also done to get a robust placebo NE.

2.2.3.2. Freeze-thaw test. For this test, in three cycles, formulations
were subjected to be stored at −21 °C and 45 °C for not less than 48 h.
2.2.3.3. Centrifugation test. Formulations were centrifuged at 5000 rpm
for 15 min using Remi R8C Laboratory Centrifuge (Mumbai, India).
Formulations experiencing phase separation were discarded after this
test (Azeem et al., 2009). Formulations that passed above tests were
further chosen for drug loading.
2.2.4. Preparation of drug loaded nanoemulsion
40 µg of LET was dissolved in selected oil followed by the addition
of surfactant mixture (Surfactant and co-surfactant = Smix). Both oil
and Smix were mixed properly using Remi cyclomixer and finally ti-
trated with HPLC water to obtain LET-NE (Ahmed et al., 2018). The
order of adding excipients is extremely crucial for the formulation of
the NE. Adding surfactants to water phase followed by adding the oil
phase leads to the development of macroscopic emulsions (Anton and
Vandamme, 2011).
2.2.5. Characterization of nanoemulsion
2.2.5.1. Droplet size, zeta potential and polydispersity index (PDI). The
droplet size, zeta potential and PDI of the developed NE were
determined by dynamic light scattering technique (Malvern Zetasizer,
Nano ZS, UK). Formulations were diluted 50 times before testing. The
analysis was carried out at 25 °C and the angle of detection was kept 90°
(Shobhit et al., 2016).

transmittance. Percentage

The pH of LET-NE was estimated by formerly calibrated pH meter

2.2.5.4. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The morphology of NE
was studied by transmission electron microscopy at AIIMS, New Delhi,
India. To measure morphology and size distribution, a drop of diluted
sample (50 times diluted) was deposited on the copper grid by
micropipette. After 2 min, the copper grid was dried and dipped in
2% w/v phosphotungstic acid. The stained grids were then placed on
filter paper in a petri dish. The stained grid was analyzed by CM 200,
Philips Briarcliff Manor, NY, USA (Kawish et al., 2017).
2.2.6. In vitro drug release
The in vitro drug release study of the developed formulation was
carried out using a dialysis membrane (MW 12,000–14,000) (Alam
et al., 2018). The release medium consists of 50 ml of phosphate buffer
(pH 6.4) and methanol (7:3) (Alexis et al., 2004). The dialysis mem-
brane was filled with 0.5 ml sample of LET-NE and LET suspension. LET
suspension was prepared by suspending LET in 0.1% aqueous mixture
of carboxymethyl cellulose. Both the ends of the membrane were sealed
to avoid leakage. The dialysis membrane was immersed in 50 ml release
medium maintained at 37 ± 1 °C and stirred constantly at 100 rpm for
8 h. At different time interval i.e. 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 h, 1 ml sample
was withdrawn from release medium and replaced with fresh 1 ml re-
lease medium to retain the sink condition. LET-NE and LET suspension
samples were analyzed spectrophotometrically at 240 nm (Shimadzu-
1800, Japan) (Sood et al., 2014).
2.2.7. Ex vivo permeation study
For drug permeation study, nasal mucosa (goat) was acquired from
the local slaughterhouse. Freshly, procured nasal mucosa was kept in
10% v/v formalin solution and stored at −20 °C. The superior nasal
conche was separated and isolated nasal mucosal membrane was wa-
shed with Phosphate buffer saline (PBS) pH 6.4. The Ex-vivo permeation
study of NE was performed by using Franz diffusion cells (LOGAN
Instruments, SFDC6S, NJ, USA). The cell cap (donor) and cell body
(receptor) compartment of each diffusion cell had a definite volume of
1 and 5 ml. The release medium (7:3 v/v PBS: methanol) was filled in
the receiver compartment. The nasal mucosa was inserted between the
donor and receiver compartment. The temperature of the receiver
compartment was fixed at 37 ± 0.5 °C under the continuous stirring
speed of 300 rpm respectively. The mounted nasal mucosa was stabi-
lized for 15 min prior to the study. Diffusion studies were conducted by
inserting LET suspended in 0.1% aqueous mixture of carboxymethyl
cellulose (LET suspension) and LET-NE in donor compartment. The
samples (1 ml) from receiver compartment were withdrawn at pre-
determined time intervals (0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 h) and quanti-
tatively analysis of drug was done by UV spectrophotometry. In the
receiver compartment, the same amount of fresh release media was
added after the removal of each sample, to retain the sink condition
(Ahmed et al., 2018; Hosny and Banjar, 2013).
2.2.8. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)
The differential scanning calorimetry was performed to determine
solubilization and complete incorporation of LET in the formulation.
The DSC thermograms of pure LET and LET-NE were recorded by DSC
apparatus (Perkin Elmer, Pyris 6 DSC, USA). The samples (1 g) of pure
LET and lyophilized LET-NE were placed in standard aluminum pans,
hermetically sealed and another pan was kept empty for reference. The
samples were scanned over a temperature range of 40 °C–200 °C at a
heating rate of 10 °C/min over and constant flow of nitrogen at 60 ml/
min. The NE was lyophilized by using 5% mannitol as a cryoprotectant.
The thermo-analytical parameters were calculated with Pyris software
(Perkin-Elmer, USA) (Khan et al., 2016b).

2.2.9. Pharmacodynamics studies
2.2.9.1. Animals. The experimental protocol (Project no. 1266, year,
2016) was approved by the Institutional Animal Ethics Committee
(IAEC) of Jamia Hamdard, New Delhi. The experimental procedures
were conducted as per the Committee for the Purpose of Control and
Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA) guidelines. Swiss albino
male mice (30–40 g, 8–10 weeks old) were obtained from Central animal
house facility, Jamia Hamdard, New Delhi. All animals were housed in
polypropylene cages under controlled conditions of temperature and
humidity (25 ± 2 °C, 55–65%) and the light–dark cycle of 12:12 h.
Animals were sustained on pellet feed with food and water ad libitum.
2.2.9.2. Experimental design. The experiments were performed in the
neurobehavioral
pharmacology
laboratory,
soundproof
room,
Jamia
Hamdard, New Delhi. We attained a sample size of 3 animals in each
group by using G* power software. However, we used 4 animals per group
taking into consideration possible mortality due to KA. KA was suspended
in sterilized normal saline while LET was dissolved in 10% DMSO. Swiss
albino male mice were selected randomly and divided into four groups
with 4 animals per group: Group I (CONTROL): received normal saline
(10 ml/kg); Group II (KA): received kainic acid (10 mg/kg, i.p.); Group III
(LET + KA): received LET + KA (1 mg/kg, i.p. + 10 mg/kg, i.p.); Group IV
(LET-NE + KA): received LET NE + KA (1 mg/kg, i.n. + 10 mg/kg, i.p.)
respectively. LET and LET-NE was given 60 min prior to KA. Drug
treatment to group I to III were administered by the intraperitoneal route
(i.p.) in a volume not exceeding 10 ml/kg. Group IV was administered LET-
NE (25 ul) in each nostril (Southam et al., 2002). The formulation was
instilled into the nostrils with the help of micropipette. The mice were held
from the back in a sloped posture for intranasal (i.n.) administration.
2.2.9.3. KA-induced status epilepticus (SE). After administration of KA,
for monitoring SE the animals were kept in separate acrylic plastic
cages and were observed for 120 min. The parameters comprised time
taken for the first onset of a seizure and a total number of seizures
(Iqbal et al., 2018). The convulsive behavior was scored corresponding
to Modified Racine’s scale (1972) as follows: Stage 0 = no changes;
Stage 1 = immobility and staring; Stage 2 = clonic head bobbing; Stage
3 = forelimb clonus and rearing; Stage 4 = rearing and falling; Stage
5 = jumping, circling and rolling; Stage 6 = generalized tonic-clonic
seizures. During seizure scoring, the person was blinded to the
treatment received by the animals. The initial beginning of head
nodding was regarded as the onset time of seizures.
2.2.9.4. Sample preparation. After monitoring animals for behavioral
seizures, animals were sacrificed after 2 h for biochemical estimation of
17β-estradiol, 5α-DHT, and 3α-Diol. The brains were separated quickly;
the hippocampi were isolated and wash out with a phosphate buffer
solution (PBS) to remove blood. PBS provides a simulation of natural
ionic strength and ion composition. Buffer solution added helps in
improving the stability of molecules as these molecules are subjected to
various forces designed to isolate them for biochemical estimations. It
also protects the integrity of the proteins, hormones while separating
them from other integrated cell components. The hippocampus was
homogenized with around 10 volumes of PBS and later centrifuged at
4 °C. The aliquots were kept at −80 °C for quantitative estimation by
ELISA.
2.2.9.5. Estimation of 17β-estradiol level. 17β-estradiol is recognized to
be proconvulsant and plays a part in the etiology of epilepsy. Aromatase
enzyme transforms testosterone into 17β-estradiol, which enhances
brain excitability (Martini et al., 1993). The quantitative estimation of
17β-estradiol was accomplished by mouse specific Elisa kit procured
from Sincere Biotech (China).
2.2.9.6. Estimation
of
5α-Dihydrotestosterone
(5α-DHT)
level. Testosterone has pronounced influence on seizure susceptibility.
It exhibits both proconvulsant and anticonvulsant actions in an animal
model
and
humans.
Testosterone
metabolizes
to
5α-

DHT level was determined in the hippocampus by mouse specific 5α-

2.2.9.7. Estimation of 3α-androstanediol (3α-Diol) level. 5α-DHT further
reduced to form 3α-androstanediol (3α-Diol) by 3α-hydroxysteroid
oxidoreductase enzyme (3α-HSOR). 3α-Diol acts on GABAA receptors
and diminishes brain excitability (Reddy and Kulkarni, 2000). The
mouse 3α-androstanediol (3α-Diol) ELISA was purchased from Sincere
Biotech (China) and was used in the quantitative estimation of the
mouse 3α-Diol in the hippocampus.
2.2.9.8. Assessment of KA-induced neurodegeneration. Neurodegeneration
in the hippocampus was ascertained by cresyl violet (CV). 24 h after drug
treatments, animals were sacrificed and the brains were isolated and were
stored in 10% formalin. Afterward, brains were fixed in paraffin wax and
were cut in serial coronal sections using microtome. Hippocampus
comprising
sections
were
deparaffinized,
rehydrated
and
stained
through
CV
(Sigma,
USA)
and
examined
for
pyknosis
of
the
hippocampus underneath an optical microscope (Olympus BX 52,
Japan). The total number of intact cells and dead cells including
pyknotic nuclei were ascertained in the CA1, CA3 and DG sub-regions
of the hippocampus in each group (Kinoshita et al., 2012). The percentage
pyknosis (pyknotic nuclei) was calculated as (total number of pyknotic
cells/total number of intact cells × 100) in different of the hippocampus.
2.2.9.9. Gamma scintigraphy studies. The drug was radiolabeled by 99m
Technetium (99mTc) using stannous chloride as a reducing agent as per
the previous report (Khan et al., 2016a). Briefly, to the weighed
quantity of the drug, 0.5 ml of an ethanolic solution of stannous
chloride and 99mTc was added and kept at 40 °C in an oven for
drying. The radioactivity was found to be 160 MBq. The radiolabeled
drug was used to prepare LET-NE formulation and LET drug solution,
by dissolving the weighed amount of radiolabelled LET in 10% DMSO
solution. The radiolabeling efficiency was determined by ITLC and
radioactivity of final formulations was again measured. The mice were
distributed into two groups (n = 3). The first group received intranasal
99m Tc-LET-NE (1 mg/kg, i.n.) and the second group received i.p.
injection of 99mTc-LET solution (LS) (1 mg/kg, i.p.). Before nasal
administration of the LET-NE, the mice were partially anesthetized
with 0.4 ml ketamine (50 mg/ml). 25 µl of solution were administered
in each nostril using micropipette. The mice were held from the back in
a tilted position during nasal administration (Mahajan et al., 2014a; Md
et al., 2013). A single photon emission computerized tomography
(SPECT, LC 75-005, Diacam, Siemens AG, Erlanger, Germany) gamma
camera was used to record images. Gamma imaging was done 30 min
post dosing and the concentration of drug in the brain was estimated by
counting radioactivity in the region of interest through software. The
results are expressed as %, which indicates the amount of radioactivity
which is determined by drawing region of interest.
2.2.9.10. Statistical analysis. Results were expressed as mean ± SEM.
Data were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed
by post hoc Tukey-Kramer multiple comparison tests. All statistical tests
were performed with GraphPad InStat software version 3.06. P < 0.05
was considered significant. Fisher’s exact test was used for analyzing %
seizure occurrence. Seizure scoring was analyzed by Kruskal-Wallis
analysis followed by multiple comparison tests.

4. Discussion
NE is a thermodynamically stable system developed using a specific
concentration of oil, Smix, and water. NE is preferred delivery system for
intranasal administration of water insoluble drugs owing to ease of
application, safety profile, high penetration and high solubilization
potential. Many researchers have developed intranasal NE formulations
for antiepileptic drugs and found enhanced drug permeation through
the olfactory pathway. NE formulations have been found to enhance
drug absorption and bioavailability of various antiepileptic drugs such
as carbamazepine, diazepam, lorazepam, and midazolam in the brain
by using the intranasal route of delivery (Kaur and Kim, 2008; Li et al.,
2002; Serralheiro et al., 2014). In our earlier study, we have shown that
aromatase inhibition by letrozole attenuates kainic acid-induced sei-
zures. In the present study, we have developed NE formulation of LET
and evaluated the same for anticonvulsant and neuroprotective effects
and compared the same against free LET against KA-induced SE in mice.
The development of NE requires apt selection and concentrations of oil,
surfactant and cosurfactant (Zhang et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2016).
The high solubility of drug in oil is an important prerequisite for the
development of NE and thus triacetin demonstrating maximum solu-
bility of LET (22.36 mg/ml) was selected as oil phase. In NE formula-
tion, combination of surfactant and co-surfactant is required for

In our study, LET-NE demonstrated nano-size range and good uni-
formity. The uniform nano-sized range particles have previously de-
monstrated improved intranasal administration (Becher, 1967). Fur-
ther, the low zeta potential value of developed LET-NE suggested good
stability of nanoemulsion (Salim et al., 2011). Transmittance is another
important parameter to predict the stability of the developed for-
mulation. It indicates the clarity of nanoemulsion. Any variation in
transmittance value indicates the change in globule size and size dis-
tribution (Polychniatou and Tzia, 2014). The results of the transmit-
tance study showed that the prepared NE is isotropic in nature. The pH
of the NE was found to be compatible with nasal mucosa exhibiting the
non-irritant nature of the formulation. The higher values of percentage
drug content indicate a higher amount of LET exists in NE formulation.
TEM images showed that the formulation droplets were of spherical
shape and the results are in agreement with the globule size distribution
measured by particle size analysis.
In, the in vitro drug release study, we have used methanol as a co-
solvent to maintain sink conditions for LET, since it has poorly aqueous
solubility. LET-NE demonstrated a significant enhancement in the drug
release compared to LET suspension. The drug release from LET-NE
indicates higher drug solubilization potential of the prepared NE. The
higher drug release from LET-NE is a result of low surface free energy at
the oil-water interface, which leads to immediate LET solubilization in
dissolution media. The enhanced release might also be due to enhanced
solubility of LET in the oil, presence of surfactant and particle size as
reported previously (Soni et al., 2018). The ex vivo permeation study of
LET-NE and LET suspension was conducted using goat nasal mucosa.
The drug permeated from LET-NE was significantly higher than LET
suspension. The enhanced permeation of drug from LET-NE might be
because of the small droplet size which leads to more drug solubiliza-
tion, which resulted in enhanced drug permeation. The enhanced drug
permeation from LET-NE may also be due to the transcellular uptake,
high solubilization capacity and enhanced absorption of the NE (Vyas
et al., 2006). The DSC thermogram of LET-NE displayed a single peak,
demonstrating that the drug was completely dispersed in the oil phase
of the developed formulation.
Further, we assessed the developed formulation for the pharmaco-
dynamics activity in KA-induced SE in mice. KA-induced seizures and
related neurotoxicity in the hippocampus is a well-known animal model
of SE. In our study, in KA-induced seizures, LET-NE was found to en-
hance the onset time of seizures, reduced seizure score and protected
100% of animals from the occurrence of KA-induced SE and the effects
were found to be more pronounced than free LET. The pharmacody-
namics study was performed to find out the plausible mechanism for
the anticonvulsant action of LET-NE on KA-induced SE. We assessed the
probability that whether inhibition of aromatase enzyme directing to
low estradiol levels or redirecting the pathway to 5α-DHT and beyond
to 3α-Diol, which is accountable for the anticonvulsant effect. LET-NE
significantly reduced the 17β-estradiol levels in the hippocampus.
Various research studies have shown the proconvulsant effects of 17β-
estradiol (Buterbaugh, 1989; Woolley, 2000). Therefore, it is probable
that the anticonvulsant effect of LET-NE is via inhibiting the conversion
of testosterone into 17β-estradiol. We further assessed the probability
of whether LET-NE mediates its action as a result of redirecting the
pathway to testosterone and further to 5α-DHT and 3α-Diol. Testos-
terone is metabolized 5α-DHT, which later reduces to form 3α-Diol. 3α-
Diol acts on GABAA receptors due to which it reduces brain excitability
(Reddy and Kulkarni, 2000). Therefore, we determined the concentra-
tions of 5α-DHT and 3α-Diol in animals. We found that LET-NE sig-
nificantly increased the levels of 5α-DHT and 3α-Diol in the hippo-
campus which shows that inhibition of aromatase by LET-NE diverted
testosterone for the production of 5α-DHT and 3α-Diol as shown by the
increased levels of 5α-DHT and 3α-Diol in the hippocampus. Our
findings are in conformity with previous research studies which de-
monstrated that inhibition in seizures takes place by a decrease in the
level of 17β- estradiol (Rashid et al., 2015; Reddy, 2004b; Sato and
Woolley, 2016). Further, such a decrease in 17β-estradiol or enhance-
ment in 5α-DHT was more with LET-NE as compared to free LET.
Hence, it is possible that brain targeting by LET-NE show higher an-
ticonvulsant action and reducing estradiol and redirecting testosterone
to 5α-DHT and 3α-Diol.
